a: Judith
p: Her name is simply the feminine of "Judah": "Jewess" or "woman of Judea".
b: The Greek Ioudeith renders Hebrew Yehudit, the feminine of Yehudah, Judah. The name means "Judean woman" or "Jewess" (Esau's Hittite wife has the same name in Genesis 26:34). A heroine called "the Jewish woman" who saves the Jewish nation invites a symbolic reading. Martin Luther suggested in his 1534 preface that the book might be a sacred poem in which Judith stands for the Jewish people and Holofernes for the godless ruler; most modern scholars agree that the name is chosen to make her a picture of her people. She does not appear in the story until chapter 8, after seven chapters of empire and siege.

a: son of Salamiel son of Sarasadai son of Israel
p: Her family tree runs back through the leader of Simeon in Numbers to Jacob himself.
b: Judith is given a longer genealogy than any woman in the Hebrew Bible: twelve generations in Vaticanus, sixteen in Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus. Its last links copy Numbers: "Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai" led the tribe of Simeon in the wilderness (Numbers 1:6; Numbers 7:36), and the Greek of Numbers spells them Salamiel and Surisadai. So Judith belongs to Simeon, the tribe whose sword she remembers in her prayer (9:2). "Israel" here is Jacob, the father of the tribes. The other Greek manuscripts and the KJV add four more names (see the variant).

a: of her own tribe and clan
p: Like Tobit's heroes, Judith married within her own clan.
b: Late books such as Tobit and Judith praise marriage inside one's own tribe and family (Tobit 4:12–13; Tobit 7:10–12). The law required it only for heiresses who inherited land, so that land stayed in the tribe (Numbers 36:6–9). Judith is a landowner (8:7), and at her death her property goes to her own and her husband's nearest kin (16:24), which fits that law.

a: the burning heat came down on his head
t: Struck down in the harvest field
p: Manasseh dies of sunstroke, like the Shunammite's son in the barley harvest.
b: Manasseh dies while overseeing the binders of sheaves at the barley harvest, in spring. The Bible has a close parallel: the Shunammite woman's son goes out to the reapers, cries "My head! My head!" (2 Kings 4:19), and dies on his mother's lap. Psalm 121:6 promises, "In the daytime the sun will not strike you." The detail gives Judith an ordinary, undramatic loss, and her long mourning begins from it.

a: three years and four months
t: Three years and four months, or six?
p: The Greek says four months; Jerome's Latin says six.
b: All the Greek copies give three years and four months. Jerome's Vulgate, made from an Aramaic copy, has annis tribus et mensibus sex, "three years and six months" (Vulgate 8:4), so the Douay-Rheims says the same. Nothing in the story depends on the number; it shows that Judith's mourning had gone on well past the usual time (compare thirty days for Moses, Deuteronomy 34:8).
orig: ἔτη τρία καὶ μῆνας τέσσαρες (etē tria kai mēnas tessares)

a: She had made herself a tent on the roof of her house
p: Flat roofs were living space; Judith lives apart there in prayer.
b: Houses had flat roofs used for sleeping, drying crops and prayer (Joshua 2:6; 1 Samuel 9:25; Acts 10:9). People built booths on them for the Feast of Booths (Nehemiah 8:16), and Absalom pitched a tent on the palace roof (2 Samuel 16:22). Judith's rooftop tent sets her apart from ordinary life, a place of mourning and prayer. The elders visit her there (8:36), and she goes down into the house only on Sabbaths and feasts (10:2). The Vulgate makes it "a private chamber in the upper part of her house, in which she abode shut up with her maids" (Douay 8:5).

a: She fasted every day of her widowhood
t: A fasting widow: Judith and Anna
p: Luke's Anna, a widow who served God "with fasting and prayer night and day", follows Judith's pattern.
b: Judith's life of fasting matches the widow Anna in the Temple, who "did not leave the temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day" (Luke 2:37), and the "real widow" of 1 Timothy 5:5, who "continues in requests and prayers night and day". Judith herself serves God "night and day" (11:17). Whether Luke knew Judith cannot be shown; both draw on a Jewish ideal of the praying widow. The Vulgate makes it "all the days of her life" (Vulgate 8:6). Whether Christians should keep fixed fast days is set out in the card on this chapter.

a: the days before the Sabbaths
p: One of the oldest uses of the word "pre-Sabbath", the name for Friday that Mark explains.
b: The Greek prosabbaton, "pre-Sabbath", is one of the earliest uses of this word; Mark 15:42 explains it as "the Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath". Judith would not fast on the Sabbath, the new moon or the feasts, or on the day before each, since those were days for joy (Isaiah 58:13; Nehemiah 8:9–12). The Mishnah later says that public fasts may not be decreed on new moons, on Hanukkah or on Purim (Mishnah Ta'anit 2:10). Judith goes beyond the rule by keeping the eves free as well.

a: and she stayed on and managed them
p: Judith runs her husband's estate herself, a rare picture of a wealthy, independent widow.
b: Israel's inheritance laws did not name the widow as an heir (Numbers 27:8–11), and the Bible usually pictures widows as poor (Exodus 22:22; Ruth 1). Judith instead controls gold, slaves, cattle and fields, with a woman steward (8:10). Jewish legal papers from Elephantine in Egypt (400s BC) show women holding and passing on property, so the picture is not impossible. The point for the story is that Judith is free: no man speaks for her, and she can act on her own.

a: she feared God greatly
p: The praise of the ideal wife in Proverbs 31 and of Job.
b: Judith is introduced by her beauty and wealth (8:7), and then by what matters most: she "feared God greatly". Of Job it is said, "He feared God and kept away from evil" (Job 1:1), and of the capable woman of Proverbs: grace is a lie and beauty a breath, but the woman who fears the LORD is the one to praise (Proverbs 31:30). The book holds the two together all the way through: her beauty will be her weapon, and her fear of God its limit (13:16).

a: her maid, who was in charge of everything she owned
p: Her nameless maid, called by several words, is her steward and only companion in the camp.
b: The Greek habra means a favorite or personal maid. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Rebekah's maids (Genesis 24:61) and the maid of Pharaoh's daughter (Exodus 2:5). The story also calls her Judith's "slave girl" (paidiskē, 10:10) and "slave" (doulē, 12:15, 19; 13:3). She is never named. She manages the estate, carries the food bag that will hold Holofernes' head (13:10), and is set free at the end (16:23). Medieval and Renaissance art often shows her holding the sack.

a: You set up this oath between God and yourselves
p: Judith's charge: by naming five days, the elders tried to force God's hand.
b: In 7:30–31 Uzziah promised to surrender if God sent no help within five days. Judith calls this testing God. The law forbids it: "Do not put the LORD your God to the test, the way you tested him at Massah" (Deuteronomy 6:16), where thirsty Israel had demanded water (Exodus 17:2). Bethulia's thirst repeats Massah. Jesus quotes the same law to refuse a test of God (Matthew 4:7). Judith's point is not that the elders prayed too boldly, but that they set terms God must meet.

a: to put God to the test
p: The same Greek verb is used for people testing God (wrong) and God testing people (right).
b: The verb peirazō means both "test" and "tempt". Judith uses it twice in one speech, to opposite effect: the elders "put God to the test" (8:12), while God "is testing us, just as he tested our ancestors" (8:25–26). Human beings may not test God, but God tests his people to show what is in their hearts (Genesis 22:1; Deuteronomy 8:2). English versions often hide the link by using "tempt" in one place and "test" in the other, as the KJV does here ("tempted God", "trieth us").

a: You cannot find the bottom of a human heart
p: Judith argues from the lesser to the greater, as Job's friends and Paul do.
b: If no one can sound the depths of another person's heart, how could anyone search out God's mind? Zophar asks Job, "Will you get to the bottom of God by searching?" (Job 11:7), and Paul makes the same move: no one knows a person's thoughts except that person's spirit, and no one knows God's thoughts except God's Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:11). Romans 11:33–34 asks, "Who has known the mind of the Lord?" (quoting Isaiah 40:13). Judith uses the argument not to silence prayer but to forbid deadlines.

a: Do not demand a pledge for the plans of the Lord our God
p: The verb is from the law of collateral: the elders treated God like a debtor.
b: The Greek enechyrazō means to take something as security for a loan. The Greek Old Testament uses it in the laws against seizing a millstone or a widow's cloak as a pledge (Deuteronomy 24:6, 17). Judith's picture is sharp: by setting a five-day term, the elders tried to hold God's plans as collateral, as if God owed them a payment by a due date.

a: For God is not like a man
t: Not a man, to be threatened
p: Judith turns Balaam's famous line in a new direction.
b: Balaam said, "God is not a man, that he should lie, / or a human being, that he should change his mind" (Numbers 23:19; compare 1 Samuel 15:29). Judith keeps the shape of the saying but changes its point: God is not a man "to be threatened", or a "son of man" (a Hebrew way of saying "a human being") "to be bargained with". The second verb, diaitaō, is used of settling a dispute by arbitration.

a: any tribe or clan or district or town of ours that bows down to gods made by hands
p: Judith speaks as a Jew after the exile, when idol worship was no longer Israel's sin.
b: Before the exile, the prophets and Kings blame Judah's fall on idolatry (2 Kings 21:10–15; 2 Kings 23:26–27). Judith says that this is in the past: "as there was in former days". That fits the book's own setting, after the return from exile (4:3), not the real age of Nebuchadnezzar, when Jeremiah was still denouncing idols in Judah (Jeremiah 7:17–18; Jeremiah 11:9–13). It also fits the book's first readers in the 100s BC. After the crisis under Antiochus IV, when some Jews did sacrifice to idols (1 Maccabees 1:43, 52), loyal Jews were proud of their faithfulness.

a: all Judea will fall too
p: The Greek says Judea "will sit"; the sense is debated.
b: The Greek kathēsetai means "will sit". It may picture Judea sitting desolate like the widowed city of Lamentations ("How lonely sits the city", Lamentations 1:1), or it may be a mistranslation of a Hebrew verb meaning "be taken". The KJV has "shall lie waste". The Plain gives the general sense, "fall". Bethulia guards the passes to Judea (4:7), so its fall would open the way to Jerusalem.
orig: καθήσεται πᾶσα ἡ Ἰουδαία (kathēsetai pasa hē Ioudaia)

a: he will demand our blood for its desecration
t: God will require it of us
p: If Bethulia surrenders, God will hold its leaders guilty for the Temple's fall.
b: To "require blood" from someone is the language of Genesis 9:5 and Ezekiel 3:18–20: God holds the watchman responsible for the lives lost through his failure. Judith turns the elders' plan around. They hoped that giving up would save lives, but the defilement of the Temple that follows would be charged to them. Sinaiticus makes "the Lord" the subject (see the variant).

a: We will be something offensive and shameful to those who own us
p: Judith echoes the covenant curses of Deuteronomy.
b: Moses warned: "You will become a sight that shocks people, an example in their sayings and a target of their jokes, among all the peoples the LORD drives you to" (Deuteronomy 28:37). Jeremiah repeats it for the exiles (Jeremiah 24:9). Judith reminds the elders that surrender would not end the suffering. It would bring exile and slavery again, the very curse the people had escaped when they came back from exile (4:3).

a: He is testing us, just as he tested our ancestors
p: Judith reads the siege as a test from God, not as a punishment, and calls for thanks.
b: Judith gives one of the clearest Jewish statements of suffering as testing. God tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1), and he tests Israel to see what is in their hearts (Deuteronomy 8:2, 16). Because Bethulia has not sinned by idolatry (8:18–20), the siege cannot be a punishment; it must be a test, and the right answer is thanks. Later Jewish and Christian writers say the same: Sirach 2:1–5 compares the testing of the faithful to gold in a furnace, and James 1:2–3 and 1 Peter 1:6–7 urge joy in trials. Whether God sends such trials or only allows them is set out in the cards at Job 2 and Job 36.

a: how he tested Isaac
p: Genesis says God tested Abraham. Judith adds a testing of Isaac, as later Jewish tradition did.
b: Genesis 22:1 says "God put Abraham to the test." It never says God tested Isaac. Judith goes beyond Genesis here, in line with Jewish tradition that made Isaac a willing sharer in the test of the binding (Genesis 22). 4 Maccabees 13:12 and 16:20 praise Isaac for giving himself to be sacrificed. This is an addition to the Genesis account, not a conflict with it. Jacob's trials "in Mesopotamia of Syria" (the Greek Old Testament's name for Aram-naharaim, Genesis 24:10) are his twenty years of hard service under Laban (Genesis 31:38–42).

a: The Lord whips those who come near him, to warn them
t: The Lord whips those he draws near
p: The Greek verb is the one Proverbs and Hebrews use for the Father's discipline.
b: The word mastigoi, "whips", is the verb of Proverbs 3:12 in the Greek Old Testament: the Lord "whips every son he receives". Hebrews 12:6 quotes that line to teach that Christians' hardships are a Father's training (Hebrews 12:5–11). Judith says something milder than punishment: God has not "taken vengeance" on Bethulia but is warning those who are close to him. Jerome's Latin expands the thought: the people should "believe that these scourges of the Lord, with which like servants we are chastised, have happened for our amendment, and not for our destruction" (Douay 8:27).

a: the shape of your heart is good
p: A Hebrew idiom: the yetser, the inclination or bent of the heart.
b: The Greek plasma tēs kardias, "the thing formed by the heart", renders the Hebrew yetser lev. Genesis 6:5 says that "every plan their hearts shaped was nothing but evil all day long". Later Jewish teaching spoke of two inclinations in each person, the good yetser and the evil one. Uzziah's compliment is that Judith's inner bent is good. This is one of many places where the Greek of Judith keeps a Hebrew way of speaking.
orig: τὸ πλάσμα τῆς καρδίας σου (to plasma tēs kardias sou)

a: to bring an oath on ourselves that we will not break
p: Uzziah will not break the oath, so Judith must work inside its five days.
b: Uzziah admits that Judith is right, but he cannot take back the oath. Israel's stories treat oaths as binding even when rash: Jephthah could not take back his vow (Judges 11:35), and Joshua kept a treaty with Gibeon that had been won by trickery (Joshua 9:19). Judith does not ask him to break it. She promises that God will act "before the days are up" (8:33). Whether a rash vow must be kept is carded at Judges 11.

a: for you are a devout woman
p: Uzziah asks Judith to do what Elijah and the rain-makers of Jewish lore did.
b: Uzziah wants rain to fill the cisterns, since the springs are held by the enemy (7:7, 17). Elijah prayed and the rain came (1 Kings 18:42–45; James 5:17–18). The Mishnah tells of Honi the Circle-Drawer, a holy man of the first century BC, whose prayers brought rain (Mishnah Ta'anit 3:8). Judith answers that she will do something else (8:32). The word for "devout", eusebēs, is a Greek word for piety, not common in the Greek Old Testament.

a: that will be told to the children of our people down through all generations
p: A Hebrew way of saying "for all time", and a promise the book itself keeps.
b: The Greek eis geneas geneōn, "to generations of generations", copies a Hebrew phrase (ledor dor), as in Psalm 72:5. Judith promises a deed that will be retold for ever, and the book about her is that retelling. Uzziah says the same of her hope at 13:19.

a: the Lord will come to the help of Israel by my hand
p: The verb is the Bible's word for God coming to rescue, and "by my hand" becomes the book's refrain.
b: The Greek episkeptomai, "visit", renders the Hebrew paqad: God "visits" his people to rescue them (Genesis 50:24; Exodus 4:31; Ruth 1:6), as Zechariah sings, "he has visited and redeemed his people" (Luke 1:68). "By my hand" runs through the book: 9:9–10; 12:4; 13:14–15; 15:10; 16:5. God's hand works through the hand of a woman.
orig: ἐπισκέψεται Κύριος τὸν Ἰσραὴλ ἐν χειρί μου

a: At that very time the incense of that evening was being offered in Jerusalem
t: Prayer at the hour of incense
p: Judith prays when the evening incense rises in the Temple, far away in Jerusalem.
b: Priests burned incense morning and evening (Exodus 30:7–8). Pious Jews timed their prayers to the Temple's offerings: "Let my prayer be set up as incense in front of you, / my hands raised high as the evening grain offering" (Psalm 141:2). Ezra knelt to pray "When the evening grain offering came" (Ezra 9:5), and Daniel at the same hour (Daniel 9:21). Luke sets Zechariah's vision at the hour of incense, while the people prayed outside (Luke 1:10). Judith joins the Temple's worship from Bethulia, and her prayer is for that Temple.

a: God of my ancestor Simeon!
t: Simeon's sword: praised here, cursed in Genesis
p: Judith praises the massacre at Shechem, which Jacob condemned on his deathbed. This conflicts with Genesis.
b: In Genesis 34, Simeon and Levi avenge their sister Dinah by tricking and killing all the men of Shechem. Jacob rebukes them (Genesis 34:30), and on his deathbed he curses their anger: "Their anger be cursed, for it was savage" (Genesis 49:7). Judith instead says God put the sword in Simeon's hand. Here the book conflicts with Genesis' own verdict. It is not alone: Jubilees 30 and the Testament of Levi 5–6 also praise the vengeance, as zeal for purity. That reading was popular in the 100s BC, when the Hasmoneans fought the Samaritans of Shechem. Some readers who hold Judith as Scripture answer that she praises the zeal against defilement, not every act.
r: Genesis 34:1–31; Genesis 49:5–7; Jubilees 30:1–6; Testament of Levi 5–6

a: For you had said, 'It must not be done,'
p: Judith quotes the brothers' outrage from Genesis 34 as God's own word.
b: Genesis 34:7 says Shechem had done "a disgraceful thing in Israel... and such a thing is not done". Judith treats that judgment as God's word ("you had said"), which makes the brothers' revenge an act of obedience. The same phrase is used of Amnon's rape of Tamar (2 Samuel 13:12).

a: and their bed, which was ashamed of their deceit, was itself deceived and stained with blood
p: A hard line in the Greek: the men who deceived Dinah were themselves deceived.
b: The Greek is difficult: literally "their bed, which was ashamed of their deceit, deceived into blood". The point is measure for measure. Shechem's men deceived (or seduced) Dinah, and Jacob's sons "answered... with trickery" (Genesis 34:13), killing them while they were weak. Judith sees God's justice in the trick. This is the precedent for her own prayer: she will ask God to use her "deceit" against a man who wants to deceive her (9:10, 13; 12:16).
orig: ἣ ᾐδέσατο τὴν ἀπάτην αὐτῶν ἀπατηθεῖσαν εἰς αἷμα

a: They burned with zeal for you
p: The zeal of Simeon, Phinehas and the Maccabees.
b: Literally, "they were zealous with your zeal", the phrase used of Phinehas, who was "zealous with my zeal" when he killed an Israelite and his Midianite partner (Numbers 25:11). Elijah says, "I have burned with zeal for the LORD" (1 Kings 19:10). In the 160s BC, Mattathias began the Maccabean revolt by killing a Jew who sacrificed to an idol, "He was zealous for the law, as Phinehas had been" (1 Maccabees 2:24–26). Judith's first readers, under the Hasmoneans, would have heard their own heroes in this praise.

a: O God, my God, hear me too, a widow
p: The law promises that God hears a widow's cry.
b: God promised, "If you do treat him harshly, and he cries out to me, be sure I will hear his cry" (Exodus 22:23), and the Psalms call God "a judge who stands up for widows" (Psalm 68:5). Judith names herself a widow twice in her prayer (9:4, 9). She asks God to act through someone the enemy would never fear.

a: The things you decided stood before you and said, 'Here we are!'
p: God's plans answer him like servants, as the lightning does in Job.
b: God asks Job, "Will you send off the lightning, and off it goes, / saying to you, 'Here we are'?" (Job 38:35). Baruch 3:34–35 says the stars answer God the same way. Judith applies the image to history: every event God plans stands ready like a servant. The second half of the verse says that God's judgment is made "with foreknowledge" (prognōsis). Judith will use the same word, with irony, when she tells Holofernes that she knows the future "by my foreknowledge" (11:19).

a: They are proud of their horses and riders
p: Judith's prayer recalls the Song of the Sea and the Psalms: God does not save by cavalry.
b: The Song of the Sea begins, "Horse and its rider he has flung into the sea" (Exodus 15:21). The Psalms say, "These have chariots, and those have horses, / but we call on the name of the LORD our God" (Psalm 20:7), and "The horse is a lie when you hope for victory" (Psalm 33:17). Isaiah warns against those who go down to Egypt and lean on horses (Isaiah 31:1). The Vulgate makes the Exodus link explicit, asking God to look on the Assyrian camp "as thou wast pleased to look upon the camp of the Egyptians" (Douay 9:6).

a: you are the Lord who shatters wars
p: Judith quotes the Greek of Exodus 15:3, which differs from the Hebrew.
b: The Hebrew of Exodus 15:3 says, "The LORD is a man of war. / The LORD is his name." The Greek Old Testament turned this into "The Lord who shatters wars; the Lord is his name". Judith quotes that Greek form here and in her song (16:2). The change makes God the one who ends wars rather than a warrior. The words "The Lord is your name" begin 9:8 in Swete's numbering; the KJV puts them at the end of 9:7. On the Greek "the Lord" for the Hebrew name, see the note at 16:2.
orig: σὺ εἶ Κύριος συντρίβων πολέμους (sy ei Kyrios syntribōn polemous)

a: to defile the tent where your glorious name rests
p: A Hebrew way of speaking of the Temple, as the dwelling of God's name.
b: Literally "the tent of the resting of the name of your glory". Deuteronomy calls the Temple the place where God will "make his name live" (Deuteronomy 12:11), and the "glory" fills it (1 Kings 8:10–11). "Tent" recalls the tabernacle, though the Temple stood in stone. The fear that the Temple would be profaned was real for the first readers. In 167 BC Antiochus IV set up "the abomination of desolation" on the altar (1 Maccabees 1:54).
orig: τὸ σκήνωμα τῆς καταπαύσεως τοῦ ὀνόματος τῆς δόξης σου

a: to hack off the horn of your altar with iron
p: The altar's horned corners were its holiest part.
b: The great altar had a horn at each corner (Exodus 27:2). Blood was put on the horns (Leviticus 4:7), and people seeking refuge took hold of them (1 Kings 1:50). To cut them off was to destroy the altar, as God threatens to do to Bethel's altar (Amos 3:14). Excavations have found horned altars in Israel, for example at Beersheba and Megiddo.

a: by the deceit of my lips
p: Judith asks God to strike the enemy through her deception. Readers have argued about it ever since.
b: Judith does not hide what she will do: she asks God himself to strike "by the deceit of my lips" (literally "from lips of my deceit", a Hebrew-style phrase), and again to use "my words and my deceit" (9:13). The striker is God; her deceit is his means. Readers have answered in very different ways. Thomas Aquinas held that every lie is a sin, and that Judith "is praised, not for lying to Holofernes, but for her desire to save the people". Others, from John Cassian to modern writers on just war, have allowed deceiving an enemy in war. Jerome's Latin removes the problem, so the Douay reads "do thou strike him by the graces of the words of my lips" (Douay 9:13). The question is set out in the chapter's deep section and in the card at Joshua 2.

a: by a woman's hand
t: By the hand of a woman
p: The phrase recalls Deborah's word about Sisera, and it returns at the climax.
b: Deborah told Barak, "the LORD will sell Sisera into a woman's hands" (Judges 4:9), and Jael killed him in her tent (Judges 4:21). Abimelech begged his armor-bearer to kill him "so no one can say about me, 'A woman killed him'" (Judges 9:54). Being killed by a woman was a great shame for a warrior. Judith asks for the same humiliation for Holofernes, and the phrase returns at 13:15 and 16:5. The Greek is en cheiri thēleias, "by the hand of a female".

a: You are the God of the lowly
p: A chain of titles for the God who saves the weak, close to Mary's song.
b: God's strength "does not lie in numbers": so Jonathan said, "He can save with many or with few" (1 Samuel 14:6), and God cut Gideon's army so that Israel could not say "My own hand rescued me" (Judges 7:2). The titles that follow, God of the lowly, helper of the least, protector of the weak, rescuer of the hopeless, belong to the Bible's great theme of reversal. Hannah sings it (1 Samuel 2:4–8) and Mary takes it up: "he has lifted up the lowly" (Luke 1:52). The same word for "lowly" appears in Judith's song (16:11).

a: Creator of the waters
p: A pointed title in a town dying of thirst.
b: Holofernes has seized Bethulia's springs (7:7, 12–17), and the people are fainting for water (7:20–22; 8:9). Judith calls on God as "Creator of the waters". The God who made the waters can give them back, or can save his people without them. In the end no rain comes: deliverance comes through her hand.

a: the house where she used to stay on the Sabbath days and on her feast days
p: On ordinary days Judith lived in her rooftop tent; on Sabbaths she came down into the house.
b: Judith's mourning and fasting belonged to weekdays (8:5–6). On the Sabbath and feasts, days of joy when she did not fast, she lived in the house below. Now, on a weekday, she goes down and dresses for a feast. Her change of clothes is the first sign that she means to act.

a: and she put on the festive clothes she used to wear while her husband Manasseh was alive
p: Judith prepares like Ruth going to Boaz and Esther going to the king.
b: Naomi tells Ruth, "So bathe, rub on scented oil, put your cloak on, and go down to the threshing floor" (Ruth 3:3). Esther puts off her mourning and puts on her royal robes before going in to the king (Esther 5:1; the Greek Additions to Esther, Addition D, makes much of her beauty). Judith follows the same pattern: bath, perfume, hair, headdress, the clothes of gladness. Each heroine risks herself before a powerful man. But Ruth seeks a husband and Esther pleads with her own husband, while Judith goes to deceive an enemy.

a: to catch the eye of any man who might see her
p: The Greek says plainly that she dressed to attract men. Jerome's Latin adds that God made her beautiful for a holy purpose.
b: The narrator does not hide Judith's aim. Some Greek copies even say she dressed "for the deceiving" of men's eyes (see the variant). Jerome's Latin adds a long defense: "And the Lord also gave her more beauty: because all this dressing up did not proceed from sensuality, but from virtue" (Douay 10:4). This line shaped Catholic preaching on Judith. Ambrose praised her for winning by sobriety and chastity rather than by charm. Modern readers are divided: some see a brave woman using the only weapon she has, others a troubling story that makes a woman's body a tool of war.

a: loaves of pure bread
p: She brings her own clean food so she will not eat Gentile food in the camp.
b: Judith takes wine, oil, roasted grain, a fig cake and "pure" loaves, bread prepared by Jews under the food laws. She will refuse Holofernes' food (12:2), as Daniel refused the king's food (Daniel 1:8) and Tobit refused "the food of the Gentiles" (Tobit 1:10–11). Jerome's list adds cheese: "and bread and cheese" (Douay 10:5). That cheese matters for the later Jewish custom of eating dairy food at Hanukkah. Medieval Hebrew retellings say she fed the enemy cheese or milk, which made him thirsty for wine, and Moses Isserles (the Rema) gives the milk as the reason for eating dairy foods at Hanukkah (see the deep section on chapter 16).

a: a cake of dried figs
p: Another wise woman once brought food, and fig cakes, out to an armed man.
b: The palathē was a cake of pressed dried figs, a long-lasting food for the road. Abigail brought "two hundred fig cakes" with bread and wine when she went out to stop David's men from killing her household (1 Samuel 25:18). Both stories are about a wise and beautiful woman who goes out to a war camp, speaks humbly to a commander, and turns the danger aside. Abigail makes peace with a future king of Israel; Judith brings death to Israel's enemy.

a: for the delight of the Israelites and the honor of Jerusalem
p: The elders' blessing uses two words that come back when Jerusalem blesses Judith (15:9).
b: The Greek gauriama means something to exult or delight in, and hypsōma means a lifting up, an exaltation. The elders pray that Judith's plan will be the Israelites' delight and Jerusalem's honor. When she comes back, the high priest and council call her by the same words: "You are Jerusalem's honor! You are Israel's great delight!" (15:9). The prayer is answered in the words it used.
orig: εἰς γαυρίαμα υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ καὶ ὕψωμα Ἰερουσαλήμ

a: her slave girl
p: The same servant is called maid, slave girl and slave.
b: The narrator calls the servant habra "maid" (8:10, 33; 10:2, 5, 17), paidiskē "slave girl" here, and doulē "slave" (12:15, 19; 13:3). The Plain keeps the different words, but it is the same woman. Judith uses doulē and paidiskē of herself when she speaks to Holofernes (11:5, 16–17). Before him she takes the place of her own maid.

a: I am a daughter of the Hebrews
p: Israelites called themselves "Hebrews" when speaking to foreigners.
b: In the Bible, "Hebrew" is the name Israelites use for themselves before outsiders, and outsiders use for them. Joseph speaks of "the land of the Hebrews" in Egypt (Genesis 40:15), Miriam speaks of "the Hebrew women" to Pharaoh's daughter (Exodus 2:7), and Jonah tells the sailors, "I am a Hebrew" (Jonah 1:9). Her first words are true. She is running from her people, but not for the reason the soldiers think. "Devoured" (literally "for food") is a Hebrew picture of utter destruction (Numbers 14:9).

a: to give him true information
p: Literally "words of truth". Judith's speeches to the enemy are full of double meanings.
b: Judith promises "words of truth" and to show Holofernes "a way". Scholars have long noticed that many of her sentences are true in a sense the hearer misses. In 11:5 she says she will not lie to "my lord", and her real Lord is God. She says God will "bring this matter to a full end" with him (11:6), and he will not "fail in his plans" until he loses his head. The irony lets the reader enjoy the trap. It also softens the charge of plain lying, though not every sentence can be saved this way: her claims about the people's sin (11:11–15) are simply false.

a: without losing one of his men, body or breath
p: A Hebrew way of saying "not one living soul".
b: The Greek says "there will not be missing of his men one flesh, nor a breath of life". "Flesh" and "breath of life" are Hebrew words for a living being, as in the Flood story: "Everything on dry land that had in its nostrils the breath of the spirit of life died" (Genesis 7:22). The Plain turns the idiom into "body or breath".
orig: σὰρξ μία οὐδὲ πνεῦμα ζωῆς (sarx mia oude pneuma zōēs)

a: they will be able to outwit the whole world
p: The soldiers' fear repeats Pharaoh's: a people that might outwit its masters.
b: The verb katasophizomai, "outwit", is the one Pharaoh uses in the Greek of Exodus 1:10: "Come on, let us outsmart them, or they will multiply still more." The soldiers decide that not one Hebrew man should be left alive, as Pharaoh ordered the killing of the boys (Exodus 1:16). Without knowing it, they have the danger in front of them: a Hebrew woman who is outwitting them already.

a: under the canopy
p: The Greek word means a mosquito net, and it is the source of the English word "canopy".
b: The Greek kōnōpion comes from kōnōps, "mosquito", and first meant a bed net hung against insects, an Egyptian fashion. Through Latin conopeum it became the English word "canopy". Holofernes' net is woven with purple, gold, emeralds and jewels, a sign of his luxury. It becomes Judith's trophy: she pulls it down (13:9), shows it at the gate (13:15), and gives it to God in the Temple (16:19).

a: She fell on her face and bowed down to him
p: Judith bows to Holofernes; Mordecai would not bow to Haman.
b: To bow face down was the honor given to kings and great men in the Near East (Genesis 42:6; 1 Samuel 25:23). In Esther, Mordecai "did not go down on his knees, and he did not bow" to Haman (Esther 3:2); the Greek Additions explain that he would give such honor to God alone (Additions to Esther 13:12–14). Judith bows without a qualm. For the book this is part of the trick, and the story does not stop to judge it.
r: Esther 3:2; Additions to Esther 13:12–14; 1 Samuel 25:23; Genesis 42:6

a: a servant of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the whole earth
p: Holofernes gives his master a title the Bible keeps for God.
b: Nebuchadnezzar's claim to be "lord of the whole earth" (2:5; 6:4) runs through the book. In the Psalms, God is "a great King over the whole earth" (Psalm 47:2). The book's question is set in 6:2: "Who is God except Nebuchadnezzar?" Judith's answer is her whole story. The real Nebuchadnezzar II ruled Babylon (605–562 BC), never Assyria, and never from Nineveh, which fell in 612 BC; the book seems to blend him with later tyrants. On the historical problem, see the book introduction.

a: I will not tell my lord a lie tonight
t: "I will not lie to my lord"
p: A sentence that is false to Holofernes and true to God.
b: This is the boldest of Judith's double meanings. Holofernes hears "my lord" as himself; the reader knows Judith's Lord is God (as in 9:12; 16:13). To Holofernes she is lying; to her God she tells no lie. Ancient and modern readers have noticed the irony; some think it clears her, others think it makes the lie worse. Compare Abraham's half-truth about Sarah (Genesis 20:12) and the midwives' answer to Pharaoh (Exodus 1:19). The moral question is set out in the deep section on chapter 9.

a: but the wild animals, the livestock and the birds of the sky will live
t: Even the animals serve the king
p: Judith flatters Holofernes in words Jeremiah and Daniel used of Nebuchadnezzar.
b: God told Jeremiah that he had put all these lands in the hand of his servant Nebuchadnezzar, and had given him even the wild animals to serve him (Jeremiah 27:6; Jeremiah 28:14). Daniel tells the king that God has put "the wild animals of the field and the birds of the sky" into his hand (Daniel 2:38). Judith's flattery borrows the language of prophecy, which the reader knows God gives and takes away.

a: Our people are not punished, and the sword does not overpower them, unless they sin against their God
t: Achior's creed, turned into a trap
p: Judith confirms what Achior told Holofernes, then uses it against him.
b: Achior had told Holofernes that Israel's God protects them unless they sin (5:17–21), the teaching of Deuteronomy and the books of Kings (Deuteronomy 28; Judges 2:11–15). Holofernes mocked him. Judith says Achior was right, and then invents the sin that will hand the people over (11:11–15). The trap works because it uses a true belief: Holofernes now waits for a sign from Israel's God.

a: the first part of the grain and the tenth of the wine and oil
p: Judith's invented sin: the starving people will eat the firstfruits and tithes kept for the priests.
b: The law gave the firstfruits and the tithes to the priests and Levites (Numbers 18:12–13, 21; Deuteronomy 18:4), and an ordinary person who ate holy food was guilty (Leviticus 22:10–16). Judith says that the people will eat the unclean animals (11:12) and the holy food. It is a sin a starving town could believably commit, and serious enough to bring God's anger. Readers in the 100s BC would think of the famine of the Maccabean wars, when food ran out in besieged Beth-zur and in the Temple fortress during a sabbatical year (1 Maccabees 6:49, 53). David ate the holy bread when he was hungry (1 Samuel 21:6), which Jesus cites (Mark 2:25–26).

a: to bring back permission from the council of elders
p: The Jerusalem council is a feature of the Persian and Greek periods, not of Nebuchadnezzar's day.
b: The Greek gerousia, "council of elders", appears with the high priest in 4:8 and 15:8. A council of elders with the high priest at its head ruled Judea under Persian and Greek kings. Antiochus III wrote to the Jewish gerousia about 200 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 12.138–142), and 1 Maccabees 12:6 names it. In the time of Jesus it was the Sanhedrin. Here it is pictured as giving rulings on law, as it did in the book's own time.

a: your slave will go out each night into the ravine and pray to God
p: Judith's nightly prayer becomes the cover for her escape.
b: Judith asks to go out each night to pray (12:6–8), and the guards learn to let her pass. On the last night she goes out "as they always did" (13:10), with the head in the food bag. The habit of prayer is real (12:8) and also part of the plan. Hannah prayed in silence and was taken for drunk (1 Samuel 1:13); Judith prays where the enemy cannot hear her.

a: You will drive them like sheep without a shepherd
p: A phrase from Moses and the prophets, here twisted into a false prophecy.
b: Moses asked for a leader so that the people would not be "like sheep with no one to shepherd them" (Numbers 27:17). Micaiah saw "all Israel scattered on the mountains like a flock with no shepherd" (1 Kings 22:17), and Jesus had compassion on the crowds because they were like that (Mark 6:34). Judith uses the image falsely, and Holofernes is the one who will lose his flock. The Assyrian army flees without its head (15:1–3).

a: not a dog will even mutter with its tongue at you
p: Judith quotes the Greek of Exodus 11:7 word for word.
b: On the night of the last plague, Moses promised that among the Israelites "not a dog will sharpen its tongue" (Exodus 11:7). Judith's words, ou gryxei kyōn tē glōssē autou, are the very words of the Greek Old Testament there. Judith takes the Exodus promise of safety for Israel and offers it, falsely, to Israel's enemy. The Greek verb gryzō means to mutter or grumble. The real Exodus-like night comes when the Assyrian camp wakes to find its leader dead (14:14–19).
orig: οὐ γρύξει κύων τῇ γλώσσῃ αὐτοῦ

a: by my foreknowledge
p: Judith claims for herself the word she used of God in her prayer.
b: The Greek prognōsis is the word Judith used of God in 9:6: "your judgment is made with foreknowledge". In the New Testament Peter speaks of Jesus handed over "by the set plan and foreknowledge of God" (Acts 2:23; 1 Peter 1:2). Before Holofernes Judith claims to be a prophetess who knows the future. The reader knows that the real foreknowledge is God's.

a: your God will be my God
p: Holofernes echoes Ruth's great vow, but as a bargain.
b: Ruth told Naomi, "Your people are my people, and your God is my God" (Ruth 1:16), and she gave up everything to say it. Holofernes offers the same words as a deal: if Judith's prophecy comes true, he will honor her God. The contrast is with Achior, an outsider who will truly come to believe in Israel's God (14:10).

a: so that it will not become a stumbling block
p: Eating Gentile food would be a "snare" that trips her into sin.
b: The Greek skandalon is a trap or something that trips a person, the word behind English "scandal". Here it means an occasion of sin: Gentile food might be unclean or offered to idols. Daniel and his friends refused the king's food for the same reason (Daniel 1:8), and so did Tobit (Tobit 1:10–11), Esther in the Greek Additions (Additions to Esther 14:17), and the faithful in 1 Maccabees 1:62–63. Paul uses the same word when he warns Christians not to put a stumbling block before others by what they eat (Romans 14:13–21).
orig: ἵνα μὴ γένηται σκάνδαλον (hina mē genētai skandalon)

a: before he has done by my hand what he has planned
p: Holofernes hears "he" as himself; the reader hears God.
b: Judith's oath "as your soul lives" sounds respectful. Her promise is double: before her food runs out, "he" will do by her hand what he has planned. Holofernes hears a promise of victory, and the reader hears the plan against him (8:33; 9:9–10). Alexandrinus spells it out by adding "the Lord" (see the variant). Abigail swears to David the same way, which the Greek of 1 Samuel 25:26 renders with the same words (ζῇ ἡ ψυχή σου).

a: bathed at the spring in the camp
p: Judith washes before she prays, a practice of Jewish piety in the Greek period.
b: The law required washing after some kinds of uncleanness (Leviticus 15). By the 100s BC many Jews also washed before prayer or meals; the Letter of Aristeas (about 150 BC) says the Jewish translators washed their hands in the sea each morning before praying (Aristeas 305–306). Stepped bathing pools for purity (mikva'ot) from the Hasmonean period have been found in Judea. Judith has lived among Gentiles in the camp and washes before she prays. That is why she comes back in "pure" (12:9). The spring is one of those that Holofernes had seized (7:7, 17).

a: Bagoas, the eunuch who was in charge of all his affairs
p: Both names belong to the Persian period, centuries after Nebuchadnezzar.
b: Bagoas is a Persian name. Diodorus of Sicily tells of a powerful eunuch Bagoas who served the Persian king Artaxerxes III (358–338 BC) on his campaign against Egypt in the 340s (Library of History 16.47–50). Elsewhere Diodorus names a Cappadocian, Holophernes, who fought in the same king's war against Egypt (Library of History 31.19.2–3, a fragment). Many scholars think the book's names come from this Persian war. Others take them as generic Persian names, since a later Cappadocian prince was also called Orophernes.

a: she will laugh at us
p: Holofernes means to have her; the story is honest about what Judith is risking.
b: Holofernes thinks it a disgrace to let such a woman go "without having been with her". The Greek is the language of sex. Her danger is the danger of Sarah before Pharaoh and Abimelech (Genesis 12:15; Genesis 20:2) and of Dinah (Genesis 34:2), the story Judith recalled in her prayer (9:2). The book insists later that he never touched her (13:16).

a: it will be my gladness until the day of my death
p: What she says sounds like flattery. The reader hears something else.
b: "Who am I to speak against my lord?" can be heard of Holofernes or of God. To do what pleases the Lord will be her joy for the rest of her life. To Bagoas this is a promise of compliance; to the reader it is Judith's vow to God, and her song (16:1–17) and long life (16:23) bear it out. Judith 12 is full of these lines (12:4, 18).

a: the fleeces she had received from Bagoas for her daily use, so that she could recline on them to eat
p: Holofernes' banquet is pictured as a Greek drinking party.
b: In the Greek world, men reclined on couches to eat and drink at a symposium. Judith reclines on fleeces spread on the ground. The picture of the drunken banquet, with the general drinking "more than... in his whole life" (12:20), belongs to the Greek age. Esther's banquets, where a king also loses his judgment over wine, are a near parallel (Esther 5:4–8; Esther 7:1–8).

a: He burned with desire to sleep with her
p: The verb for "seduce" is the same as Judith's word for her own "deceit".
b: The Greek here is apataō, to deceive or to seduce. Holofernes had been waiting "to seduce her" (literally "to deceive her"). Judith prayed for God to use "my deceit" (apatē, 9:10, 13), and her song says she put on linen "to deceive him" (16:8). Both are trying to deceive each other, and the one who means seduction is the one deceived. The Greek of Exodus 22:16 uses the same verb for seducing a virgin.

a: for today my life means more to me than on any day since I was born
p: A line with two meanings, like her others.
b: Literally "my life was made great in me today more than all the days since my birth". Holofernes hears that she is honored to dine with him. The reader hears that this is the day of her great deed. David used similar words to Saul: "as your life counted for much in my eyes today..." (1 Samuel 26:24).

a: for he was soaked in wine
p: Drunkenness delivers the enemy into her hand, as in other Bible stories of tyrants.
b: Elah king of Israel was killed while drinking himself drunk (1 Kings 16:9–10), and Absalom's men struck down Amnon once he was merry with wine (2 Samuel 13:28). Belshazzar's feast ended with his death the same night (Daniel 5:30). Proverbs warns, "Wine is a mocker" (Proverbs 20:1). 1 Maccabees 16:16 tells of the murder of Simon, the Hasmonean high priest, while drunk at a banquet in 134 BC, which was within living memory for the book's first readers.

a: to bring honor to Jerusalem
p: Judith prays silently "in her heart", like Hannah.
b: Judith prays "in her heart", as Hannah did: "Her lips were trembling, but no one could hear her voice" (1 Samuel 1:13). Her two short prayers (13:4–5, 7) ask God to "look upon what my hands are doing" and "make me strong", a prayer like Samson's before his death: "Give me strength, please, just this one time" (Judges 16:28). Samson too was blinded and mocked by the enemy he killed.

a: took down his sword from it
p: Like David, Judith kills the enemy with his own sword.
b: David killed Goliath and then "He took hold of the man's sword, pulled it out of its sheath and finished him off, and he cut off his head with it" (1 Samuel 17:51). Judith takes Holofernes' own sword from the bedpost. A champion is beheaded with his own weapon, by someone no one feared. The story also recalls Ehud, who killed a fat king alone in a locked room and escaped while the servants waited outside (Judges 3:20–25).

a: Then with all her strength she struck him twice in the neck and took off his head
p: The story celebrates the killing. Readers have asked what kind of violence it blesses.
b: The narrative is brief and unflinching: two blows, and the head is off. Holofernes was the enemy commander of an army besieging a starving town, and he was about to destroy Judea (2:7–13). Most Jewish and Christian readers in history praised Judith as a deliverer like Jael and David. Christian writers mostly used her as a picture of chastity and courage, or of the soul defeating evil. Modern readers, after centuries of violence in God's name, are more troubled. They ask whether a story that prays for God's help to deceive and kill can be copied. The chapter's deep section sets out these readings.

a: who put it in her food bag
p: The bag that kept her clean food now hides the head.
b: The Greek does not say who put the head in the bag; the KJV has "she", and the Plain takes it to be the maid, who was handed the head in 13:9. The bag held her pure food and kept her from eating the enemy's (10:5; 12:2). Now it carries his head through the camp. The sentries let her pass because they have seen her go out with the maid and the bag every night. Renaissance painters such as Andrea Mantegna and Artemisia Gentileschi often show the maid holding the bag open.

a: God, our own God, is with us
p: Judith's shout is the meaning of the name Immanuel.
b: "God is with us" is the meaning of Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 8:8, 10; Matthew 1:23) and the refrain of Psalm 46: "The LORD of Armies is with us" (Psalm 46:7). Judith shouts it at the gate before she has said what she did, and it changes the town's despair.

a: The Lord has struck him down by a woman's hand
t: The head shown at the gate
p: Heads of defeated enemies were displayed, as David showed Goliath's.
b: David carried Goliath's head to Jerusalem (1 Samuel 17:54), and the Philistines fastened Saul's corpse to the wall of Beth-shan (1 Samuel 31:9–10). In 1 Maccabees the Jews cut off the head and right hand of the Seleucid general Nicanor and hung them up near Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 7:47; 2 Maccabees 15:30–35). Readers in the 100s BC kept a festival for that victory, Nicanor's Day, on the 13th of Adar. Judith's first readers would likely have known that event.

a: but he did no sin with me to make me unclean and ashamed
p: Judith insists she was not defiled, and Jerome's Latin adds an angel.
b: The book is careful: "my face deceived him", but he did not sin with her. Her chastity is the book's answer to the question that hangs over chapters 10–12. Jerome's Latin expands the verse: "his angel hath been my keeper both going hence, and abiding there, and returning from thence hither: and the Lord hath not suffered me his handmaid to be defiled" (Douay 13:20). The Catholic tradition took this up in seeing Judith as a figure of purity.

a: you are blessed by God Most High above all the women on earth
p: Uzziah blesses Judith as Deborah blessed Jael and Melchizedek blessed Abraham. Elizabeth's greeting to Mary is close.
b: Uzziah's blessing joins two older ones. Deborah sang, "Blessed above women be Jael" (Judges 5:24), and Melchizedek said, "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, maker of heaven and earth. / And blessed be God Most High, who has handed your enemies over to you" (Genesis 14:19–20). Elizabeth greets Mary, "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!" (Luke 1:42). This is why Catholic and Orthodox readers have long heard Judith's blessing as a type of Mary's. The Catholic use of this verse in the liturgy is set out in the card on chapter 15.

a: who led you to wound the head of our enemies' chief
p: Christian readers linked the blow to the head with the promise of Genesis 3:15.
b: God told the serpent, "He will strike you on the head" (Genesis 3:15). The Psalms speak of God striking "the head of his enemies" (Psalm 68:21; Psalm 110:6). Jael struck Sisera's head with a tent peg (Judges 5:26). Medieval Christian writers, as in the Speculum humanae salvationis (1300s), read Judith's blow to Holofernes' head as a picture of the promise in Genesis 3:15, fulfilled in Christ, and Catholic tradition applied it to Mary. That reading is typology, not the original sense of the verse.

a: because you did not hold back your own life when our people were humbled
p: Courage that risks one's own life for the people.
b: Esther said, "If I perish, I perish" (Esther 4:16). Deborah's song praises Zebulun, who "threw their lives away to the death" (Judges 5:18). Judith's courage is praised for the same reason. Christian readers later compared it to the love that lays down its life for others (John 15:13).

a: "So be it! So be it!"
p: The Greek translates the Hebrew "Amen, amen".
b: The Greek Genoito, genoito, "may it be", is how the Greek Old Testament often translates the Hebrew amen (as in Psalm 41:13, where the site has "Amen and amen"). The people answer Uzziah's blessing as a congregation in worship, as in Nehemiah 8:6. They answer again at 15:10.

a: Take this head and hang it on the battlements of your wall
p: Displaying an enemy's head on the wall was a public sign of victory.
b: The Philistines hung Saul's body on the wall of Beth-shan (1 Samuel 31:10). Assyrian palace reliefs show heads of enemies hung on city walls or piled up. Judah Maccabee hung Nicanor's head in sight of Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 7:47). Here the head becomes a weapon: when the Assyrians see Israel come out against them, they will find their leader dead (14:3).

a: But do not go down
p: Judith plans a feint: armed men march out, but do not attack.
b: Judith's plan is a military trick. The Israelites pretend to attack, the Assyrians rush to wake their general, and they find him dead. This is how God often gives victory to the few in Judges: by panic in the enemy camp (Judges 7:19–22; 1 Samuel 14:15–20).

a: call Achior the Ammonite to me
p: Achior is brought to see what he had foretold.
b: Achior had warned Holofernes that Israel's God would protect them (5:5–21), and Holofernes had sent him to Bethulia to die with them (6:10–13). Now Achior sees the head of the man who mocked him. The scene finishes Achior's part, which began in chapter 5.

a: he fell on his face, and his spirit left him
p: Literally "his spirit left him", a Hebrew-style way of saying he fainted.
b: The phrase is like the Hebrew of 1 Kings 10:5, where the queen of Sheba saw Solomon's court and, literally, there was no more spirit in her; the site's Plain renders it "It left her breathless". The Plain keeps the picture.
orig: ἐξελύθη τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ (exelythē to pneuma autou)

a: Blessed are you in every tent of Judah
p: Achior's blessing recalls Deborah's blessing of Jael "in the tent".
b: Deborah sang that Jael should be blessed above women in the tent (Judges 5:24). Achior blesses Judith "in every tent of Judah" and among every nation. "Tents" is an old word for homes in Israel (1 Kings 12:16).

a: He had the flesh of his foreskin circumcised
p: An Ammonite joins Israel, though Deuteronomy 23:3 bars Ammonites from the assembly. The two conflict.
b: Deuteronomy 23:3 says: "No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD. Even to the tenth generation, none of their descendants may ever enter the assembly of the LORD." Nehemiah enforced that law (Nehemiah 13:1–3). Judith says Achior "was joined to the house of Israel, to this day". On its face this conflicts with Deuteronomy. Jewish law later solved the problem in its own way. The Mishnah tells of an Ammonite convert, Judah, who was allowed to marry into Israel, because the Assyrian king Sennacherib had "mixed up the nations" so that the old Ammonites no longer existed (Mishnah Yadayim 4:4; the Talmud, Berakhot 28a). The Talmud also limited the ban to men and to marriage (Yevamot 76b–77a), which is how Ruth the Moabite could enter Israel. Achior is the clearest example in Jewish literature of this period of a Gentile who "believes" and is circumcised, like the converts of Esther 8:17.

a: he believed in God completely
p: Achior believes first and is circumcised after, the order Paul stresses for Abraham.
b: Achior "believed in God" and then was circumcised. Genesis says that "Abram put his trust in the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6), long before he was circumcised (Genesis 17). Paul builds on that order (Romans 4:9–12). Judith and Paul agree that faith comes first, but for Judith circumcision is the needed sign of joining the people, as it was for converts in the Hasmonean period. Josephus says the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus made the Idumeans be circumcised about 125 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 13.257–258).

a: The slaves have dared to come down to fight us
p: The Assyrians call the Israelites "slaves", which they will soon not be.
b: To the Assyrians, the Israelites are only rebel slaves of their king. The word comes back in Bagoas' cry: "The slaves have broken faith!" (14:18). Deuteronomy reminds Israel that they were slaves in Egypt and God set them free (Deuteronomy 5:15). In this story the "slaves" defeat their masters.

a: One Hebrew woman has brought shame on the house of King Nebuchadnezzar
p: The enemy states the book's point: a single woman has shamed an empire.
b: Bagoas' cry is the story in a sentence. Nebuchadnezzar claimed to be lord of the whole earth (2:5), and "one Hebrew woman" has brought him shame. Holofernes' body lies on the ground, his head gone. The scene recalls Dagon fallen before the ark with its head cut off (1 Samuel 5:4).

a: Trembling and fear fell on them
p: Fear falls on the enemy, as in the Song of the Sea.
b: The Song of the Sea says, "Terror and dread fall on them" (Exodus 15:16), and God promises, "I will send my terror before you" (Exodus 23:27). In Judges and 1 Samuel the enemy panics and flees (Judges 7:22; 1 Samuel 14:15). Judith's plan works through the same panic.

a: Those in Gilead and in Galilee outflanked them
p: The whole land joins the chase, including regions the Hasmoneans brought back into Jewish rule.
b: The chase runs from Bethulia north past Damascus, with fighters from Gilead (east of the Jordan) and Galilee. In the Maccabean wars, Judah and Simon rescued the Jews of Gilead and Galilee (1 Maccabees 5:9–23), and later Hasmonean kings brought these regions under Jewish rule. The book's picture of "all Israel" fighting together suits that time.

a: Joakim the high priest and the council of elders
p: The high priest leads the nation, as in the Persian and Hasmonean periods.
b: Joakim (4:6, 8) is the high priest who organized the defense. No high priest is named in Kings during Nebuchadnezzar's reign, but Nehemiah 12:10, 26 names a high priest Joiakim after the exile, the son of Jeshua. In the book, the high priest acts as the head of the nation, as he did under the Persians and Greeks and especially under the Hasmoneans, who were both high priests and rulers.

a: You are Jerusalem's honor! You are Israel's great delight! You are our people's great boast!
p: The leaders' praise, later sung of Mary in Catholic worship.
b: The high priest and council praise Judith with three titles: Jerusalem's "honor" (or exaltation), Israel's "great delight" and the people's "great boast". They fulfill the elders' prayer at 10:8. In the Latin these lines read Tu gloria Jerusalem; tu lætitia Israël; tu honorificentia populi nostri (Vulgate 15:10). The Roman Catholic liturgy sings them of Mary, especially on the feast of the Immaculate Conception, in the antiphon Tota pulchra es. Protestant churches do not use them this way. See the card on this chapter.

a: some of them performed a dance in her honor
p: Victory songs and dances led by women, as with Miriam and the women who greeted David.
b: After the Sea, "Then Miriam the prophet, Aaron's sister, took the hand drum in her hand, and all the women went out after her with hand drums and with dancing" (Exodus 15:20). Jephthah's daughter came out dancing (Judges 11:34), and the women greeted Saul and David with songs and dancing (1 Samuel 18:6–7). Judith leads the women as Miriam did and then sings, as Miriam and Deborah did (Exodus 15:21; Judges 5:1).

a: leafy wands
p: The Greek word is the thyrsus, the wand of Dionysus. The Maccabees carried them at the Temple's rededication.
b: The Greek thyrsos was a staff wreathed with ivy or vine leaves, carried in the processions of Dionysus. It is not a Jewish symbol in the older books. But 2 Maccabees 10:7 says that when Judah Maccabee purified the Temple in 164 BC, the people carried thyrsi, leafy branches and palms and sang hymns, at the first Hanukkah. Judith's procession uses the same word. That has suggested to many scholars that the book was written for readers who knew those celebrations. The olive garlands (15:13) were also a Greek sign of victory.

a: Strike up for my God with tambourines
p: Judith's song is modeled on the Song of the Sea and the Song of Deborah.
b: Like Miriam (Exodus 15:20–21) and Deborah (Judges 5), Judith sings of a victory God gave by unlikely means. The song has three parts: a call to praise (16:1–2), the story of the victory (16:3–12), and a hymn to God the creator and judge (16:13–17). The opening call to "tambourines" and "cymbals" sounds like Psalm 150:4–5 and Psalm 149:3. Many scholars think the song was composed in Hebrew, perhaps before the story around it.

a: For the Lord is a God who shatters wars
p: Greek has "the Lord" for God's Hebrew name, so the Plain does too.
b: In the Greek Old Testament Kyrios, "Lord", stands for God's personal name, YHWH. The site prints "the LORD" in small capitals only in translations of the Hebrew. Judith survives in Greek, so its Kyrios is "the Lord". Here Judith quotes Exodus 15:3 in its Greek form (see the note at 9:7).
orig: θεὸς συντρίβων πολέμους Κύριος (theos syntribōn polemous Kyrios)

a: Into his camp, among the people
p: A hard phrase: whose camp? The Plain follows the Greek.
b: The Greek reads "for into his camps in the midst of the people he took me out of the hand of those pursuing me". "His" may be God's (God's camp is his people) or Holofernes' (God brought her safely into the enemy camp). The KJV (its 16:3) reads "for among the camps in the midst of the people he hath delivered me". The Plain leaves the ambiguity.
orig: ὅτι εἰς παρεμβολὰς αὐτοῦ ἐν μέσῳ λαοῦ

a: Assyria came down from the mountains of the north
p: The prophets' foe "from the north".
b: Jeremiah warned of disaster coming "from the north" (Jeremiah 1:14; Jeremiah 6:22), and Ezekiel's Gog comes "from the far north" (Ezekiel 38:15). Joel calls the invader "the northerner" (Joel 2:20). The book's Assyrians play the part of that enemy from the north.

a: by a woman's hand
t: The shame of Sisera and Abimelech
p: The song repeats the book's refrain.
b: See 9:10 and 13:15. In the Song of Deborah, Jael's deed is sung in detail (Judges 5:24–27). Judith's song tells her deed in the third person, as a story about "Judith, Merari's daughter" (16:6–9), and then turns back to praising God.

a: no sons of Titans struck him down
p: The song names the Titans of Greek myth beside the giants of the Bible.
b: The Greek names "sons of Titans" and "tall giants". The Titans were the old gods of Greek myth whom Zeus overthrew. The Greek Old Testament uses "Titans" once for the Rephaim (2 Samuel 5:18), and "giants" for the Nephilim of Genesis 6:4 and the Anakim (Deuteronomy 2:10–11). The song's point is simple: no mighty warrior killed Holofernes, only a woman. Its use of the Titans shows that its translator, or poet, knew Greek ideas.

a: unstrung him with the beauty of her face
p: The verb means to loosen or paralyze.
b: The Greek paralyō, to loosen or paralyze (from which comes "paralysis"), pictures a warrior whose limbs give way. Her beauty disabled him before her sword killed him (16:9).

a: and put on a linen gown to deceive him
p: Even the song of praise says she dressed to deceive.
b: The song repeats what the story said (10:4; 12:16): she put on linen "to deceive him". Judith and the poet see no shame in it. In the Greek, the deceit of 9:10, 13, the seduction of 12:16 and the trick of 16:8 all use the same word. Her widow's clothes are taken off "to lift up those who suffered in Israel" (16:7). The motive is the rescue of the people, which is where Aquinas located her praise.

a: Her sandal caught his eye
p: A tiny detail that brings down a giant.
b: The Song of Songs praises the bride's feet in sandals (Song of Songs 7:1). The song moves in three lines from sandal to soul to sword: the smallest thing leads to the end of the mighty one. The sword went "through his neck", as told in 13:8.

a: The Persians shuddered at her daring
p: The song speaks of Persians and Medes, not Babylonians.
b: The story's enemy is "Assyria" under "Nebuchadnezzar", but here the song names Persians and Medes as the nations who heard and feared. Arphaxad, whom Nebuchadnezzar defeated in chapter 1, was king of the Medes. The names fit the Persian period, from which the names Holofernes and Bagoas also seem to come (see the note at 12:11).

a: and my weak ones were afraid and trembled
p: The Greek is unclear whether Israel's weak ones or the enemy feared.
b: The Greek reads literally: "Then my lowly ones shouted, and my weak ones feared and they were terrified; they raised their voices and they were overturned." It may mean that Israel's weak ones were afraid, or, as many think, that a Hebrew original said that the enemy feared when the weak shouted. The KJV has "my weak ones cried aloud; but they were astonished". The Plain keeps the Greek order and adds "the enemy" in the last line, since those overturned must be the Assyrians.
orig: ἐφοβήθησαν οἱ ἀσθενοῦντές μου (ephobēthēsan hoi asthenountes mou)

a: they wounded them like the children of runaways
p: The song mocks the enemy: boys and the children of runaway slaves beat them.
b: The enemy was cut down by "sons of young girls", that is, mere boys, and wounded "like children of runaways", perhaps runaway slaves, people who would not fight back. The insult is that the great army was beaten by the least of Israel.

a: I will sing a new song to my God
p: The "new song" of the Psalms, sung for a new act of God.
b: "Sing a new song to the LORD" (Psalm 96:1; Psalm 98:1; Psalm 149:1). Isaiah 42:10 calls for a new song for God's new deeds, and Revelation's redeemed "sang a new song" (Revelation 5:9). Judith's hymn to the creator (16:13–17) widens her victory song into praise of God's power over all creation.

a: You sent out your spirit, and it built them
p: God made all things by his word and his breath.
b: "For he said it, and it was" (Psalm 33:9), and "You send your breath out, and they are created" (Psalm 104:30). Judith's word for "built" is the one used for God's building the woman from Adam's rib (Genesis 2:22). The Greek pneuma is God's breath or spirit, so the Plain writes "spirit" in lower case. Christian readers saw here the work of the Holy Spirit in creation, as they did in Genesis 1:2 and Psalm 33:6.

a: rocks will melt like wax at your presence
p: The language of God's coming in judgment.
b: "Like wax, the mountains melt away in the LORD's presence" (Psalm 97:5; compare Micah 1:4). Mountains shake at God's coming (Psalm 18:7; Habakkuk 3:6). But the God who melts mountains is merciful to those who fear him (Psalm 103:11, 13).

a: All sacrifice is too little to be a soothing smell
t: Fearing God is worth more than sacrifice
p: Judith's song puts fear of God above offerings, as the prophets and Psalms do.
b: "You take no pleasure in a sacrifice, or I would bring one" (Psalm 51:16), and a broken spirit is what God wants (Psalm 51:17). Samuel said, "listening is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22), and Hosea and Micah say the same (Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6–8). "Soothing smell" is the phrase of the sacrificial laws (Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9). Judith does not reject sacrifice; the people offer it at once in Jerusalem (16:18). The point is that no offering is worthy of God compared with fear of him.

a: He will put fire and worms into their flesh
p: The song ends with lasting punishment for the enemy nations. It goes beyond Isaiah, whom it echoes.
b: The last lines echo the end of Isaiah, where the corpses of the rebels lie outside Jerusalem, "for their worm will not die, and their fire will not be put out" (Isaiah 66:24). In Isaiah these are dead bodies. Judith goes beyond Isaiah: the nations "will weep and feel it forever", a punishment they feel. This is one of the earliest Jewish texts to speak of eternal conscious punishment, alongside Daniel 12:2 and 1 Enoch. Sirach 7:17 also mentions "fire and worm". Jesus quotes Isaiah's line of Gehenna (Mark 9:48). Whether the punishment of the wicked is eternal is carded at Jude 1 and 1 Enoch 108.

a: As soon as the people were purified
p: Those who had touched the dead had to be cleansed before entering the Temple.
b: The law says that soldiers who had killed or touched the dead must purify themselves for seven days (Numbers 31:19–24; Numbers 19:11–12). The people cleanse themselves before they worship at the Temple. The picture of the victors coming up to Jerusalem with offerings is like the Maccabees' return (1 Maccabees 4:24, 55–56).

a: as a dedicated offering
p: The canopy goes to the Temple as a votive gift.
b: The Greek anathēma here means a gift set up in a temple, as in Luke 21:5, where the Temple is adorned "with beautiful stones and gifts". (Some copies have the form anathema, which in the Greek Old Testament can mean a thing devoted to destruction; see the variant.) Goliath's sword was kept at the sanctuary at Nob (1 Samuel 21:9). Judith keeps none of the trophies for herself.

a: for three months
p: The rejoicing goes on far longer than any festival in the law.
b: Israel's feasts lasted seven or eight days (Leviticus 23). Solomon and Hezekiah doubled feasts to fourteen days (1 Kings 8:65; 2 Chronicles 30:23). Three months of feasting is an exaggeration that shows how great the deliverance was. The Vulgate adds that "the day of the festivity of this victory is received by the Hebrews in the number of holy days" (Douay 16:31), which the Greek does not say. No such feast is known from Jewish sources; see the deep section on the link with Hanukkah.

a: Many men desired her, but no man slept with her
p: Judith never married again. Christians made her a model of holy widowhood.
b: Judith was free to remarry; the law allowed and often encouraged it (Ruth 3–4; Deuteronomy 25:5). She chose to stay a widow for about seventy years. Paul told the widow that she was free to marry, but, in his judgment, more fortunate if she stays as she is (1 Corinthians 7:39–40), and he praised the widow who gives herself to prayer (1 Timothy 5:5). Ambrose of Milan and Jerome both held up Judith as a model for Christian widows. Jerome's Latin adds that "chastity was joined to her virtue" (Douay 16:26). Whether lifelong widowhood or celibacy is a higher calling is set out in the card on this chapter.

a: and lived to be a hundred and five
p: A long life, the reward of the righteous.
b: Long life is the Bible's reward for the righteous (Proverbs 3:1–2; Psalm 91:16). Judith lives to 105. If she was a young widow at the siege, she lived some seventy more years. During that time, the book says, no one threatened Israel. The book's setting, with Nebuchadnezzar (who died in 562 BC) ruling while the exiles have already returned (4:3), cannot be fitted to any real reign, which suggests that its history is not meant to be literal.

a: She set her maid free
p: Judith frees her slave before she dies.
b: The law commanded release of a Hebrew slave after six years (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12–15) and gave rules for freedom. Judith frees the maid who shared her danger, a reward for faithfulness. Sirach 7:21 urges masters not to deny a wise slave his freedom.

a: No one made the Israelites afraid again in Judith's lifetime
p: The book ends like the stories of the judges.
b: The judges' stories end with peace for the land: "And the land was quiet for forty years" (Judges 5:31; Judges 3:11, 30). Judith ends the same way, as a judge of Israel. Vaticanus ends the book with "Amen", as a reading for worship would end; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus do not have it (see the variant).

a: the enemy
p: The Greek has no subject here; the Plain supplies "the enemy".
b: The last line reads literally "they raised their voice, and they were overturned". The Greek does not say who was overturned. Since Israel's lowly ones are the ones who shout, those overturned must be the Assyrians, and the Plain supplies "the enemy" to make that clear. See the note on the line before.
orig: ὕψωσαν τὴν φωνὴν αὐτῶν καὶ ἀνετράπησαν
